pages.title: Stress responses
pages.visualNotes: Homeostatic cell under stress may adapt or undergo injury. Injury is reversible or irreversible (cell death); severe or progressive stress leads to irreversible injury. Removal of stress allows return from reversible injury.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Stages of cell injury
pages.visualNotes: Normal cell/homeostasis -> stress -> adaptation. Inability to adapt -> injury. Mild transient injury -> reversible injury -> normal cell. Severe progressive injury -> irreversible injury -> necrosis or apoptosis (cell death).
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Adaptive responses diagram
pages.visualNotes: Normal cells: reversible changes in size/number -> hyperplasia, hypertrophy, atrophy; reversible changes in structure/type -> dysplasia or metaplasia. pages.title: Cell injury morphology diagram
pages.visualNotes: Healthy cell Na/K ATPase exchanges 3 Na outward and 2 K inward. Hypoxia and ATP reduction accompany reversible cell/organelle swelling, detached ribosomes, chromatin clumping, blebbing, myelin figures; intracellular Na/osmotic pressure and Ca rise, K decreases. Irreversible injury: membrane rupture, nuclear pyknosis/karyorrhexis/karyolysis, vacuolization, amorphous mitochondrial densities, lysosomal rupture -> cell lysis.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Mechanisms overview diagram
pages.visualNotes: Injurious stimulus e.g. ischemia -> ATP reduction -> loss of energy-dependent functions; mitochondrial membrane damage -> cell death; lysosomal damage -> enzymatic digestion; plasma membrane damage -> lost cellular contents; increased Ca and ROS -> protein breakdown and DNA damage.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Biochemical injury pathways
pages.visualNotes: Mitochondrial damage -> ATP decrease and ROS increase (lipid/protein/DNA damage). Ca entry -> mitochondrial permeability increase and cellular enzyme activation. Plasma membrane damage -> lost components; lysosomal membrane damage -> digestion. Protein misfolding/DNA damage -> pro-apoptotic protein activation.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Calcium homeostasis
pages.visualNotes: Ca influx from extracellular space and release from mitochondria/smooth ER increases cytosolic Ca. Phospholipase -> decreased phospholipids; protease -> disrupted membrane/cytoskeleton proteins; these cause membrane damage. Endonuclease -> nuclear damage. ATPase -> decreased ATP. Ca also increases mitochondrial permeability transition -> decreased ATP.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: ATP pathways and functions
pages.visualNotes: Mitochondrial diagram labels outer/inner membrane, cristae, matrix, intermembrane space, DNA, ribosome and granule. Size markers 0.1–0.5 micrometers and 1–2 micrometers are reproduced as shown, without interpreting an unlabeled dimension.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction
pages.visualNotes: Increased cytosolic calcium, oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation -> mitochondrial injury/dysfunction. Mitochondrial permeability transition -> membrane potential loss -> inability to generate ATP -> necrosis. Cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic protein release -> apoptosis.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Mitochondrial cell death pathways
pages.visualNotes: Low O2, toxins, radiation -> mitochondrial dysfunction -> ATP decrease and ROS increase -> multiple abnormalities -> necrosis. Reduced survival signals or DNA/protein damage -> pro-apoptotic proteins increase and anti-apoptotic proteins decrease -> mitochondrial protein leakage -> apoptosis.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: Consequences of ATP depletion
pages.visualNotes: Ischemia -> oxidative phosphorylation decrease -> ATP decrease. Na pump reduction -> influx Ca, water, Na and K efflux -> ER/cellular swelling, microvillus loss, blebs. Anaerobic glycolysis increases -> glycogen decreases and pH falls -> chromatin clumping. Ribosome detachment -> protein synthesis decrease -> lipid deposition.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: ROS generation
pages.visualNotes: Mitochondrial electron transport produces superoxide; + NO -> peroxynitrite (ONOO−); SOD converts superoxide to H2O2; Fenton reaction yields hydroxyl radical. Phagocyte oxidase uses NADPH/O2 to generate superoxide in phagosomes; MPO is connected to HOCl production. Caption names NO nitric oxide; SOD superoxide dismutase.

pages.title: ROS sources and targets
pages.visualNotes: Sources: ER P450/b5 oxidases; mitochondrial P450/b5 oxidases and respiratory chain oxidation; plasma membrane NADPH oxidase; cytosolic xanthine oxidase and transition metals Cu/Fe; peroxisomal oxidases; phagocyte lysosome myeloperoxidase/NO synthase. Targets: membrane lipid peroxidation, DNA fragmentation, protein cross-linking/fragmentation. Fenton, SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidase/reductase pathways shown. Membrane antioxidants E/A/beta-carotene; cytosolic SOD, vitamin C, glutathione peroxidase, ferritin, ceruloplasmin; mitochondrial SOD/glutathione peroxidase; peroxisomal catalase.
pages.sourcePath: ../sources/slides/2.CH 1 - Cell injury I causes and targets 4.pdf

pages.title: ROS injury and removal
pages.visualNotes: Radiation/toxins/reperfusion -> ROS: superoxide -> H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical. Lipid peroxidation -> membrane damage; protein modification -> breakdown/misfolding; DNA damage -> mutation. SOD converts superoxide to H2O2; glutathione peroxidase/catalase decompose H2O2 to water. Caption: spontaneous decay and enzymatic removal limit radicals; excessive production or inadequate removal causes accumulation/injury.

pages.title: Intrinsic and extrinsic pathways

pages.title: Mitochondrial and death receptor pathways
pages.visualNotes: Intrinsic mitochondrial route: growth-factor withdrawal, DNA damage, protein misfolding/ER stress -> Bcl2 sensors/effectors Bax/Bak (inhibited by Bcl2/BclXL) -> cytochrome c/pro-apoptotic proteins. Extrinsic death receptor Fas/TNF -> adaptor proteins -> initiator caspases. Both -> executioners -> endonuclease/nuclear fragmentation and cytoskeleton breakdown -> bodies/phagocytosis.

pages.title: Survival signals versus apoptosis
pages.visualNotes: Survival signal -> Bcl2/BclXL -> no cytochrome c leakage -> survival. Lack of survival signal, irradiation/DNA damage or misfolded proteins -> sensors -> Bcl2 antagonism and Bax/Bak channel activation -> cytochrome c leakage -> caspases -> apoptosis.

pages.title: Microbial recognition and inflammasome
pages.visualNotes: Recognition diagram: extracellular bacterial cell-wall lipid via TLR and fungal polysaccharide via lectin; cytosolic bacterial lipid and viral RNA; endosomal microbial DNA/RNA via TLR lead to cytokines (TNF) and increased adhesion molecules, producing acute inflammation. pages.title: Mediator sources illustrated

pages.title: Cytokine sources and functions
pages.visualNotes: Table: IL-1 from macrophages (main), endothelial cells and some epithelial cells; TNF from macrophages/T cells. IL-1 stimulates hypothalamic CRH -> pituitary ACTH -> adrenal cortisol; PGE2 synthesis in anterior hypothalamus causes fever; hepatic APR synthesis, endothelial adhesion molecules, Th17 differentiation. TNF: apoptosis, endothelial/neutrophil activation, cachexia. IL-6 from macrophages/endothelial/T cells: primary increased hepatic APR synthesis (e.g. C-reactive protein), Th17 differentiation and B-cell proliferation. IL-8 from macrophages/epithelial/endothelial/airway smooth muscle: neutrophil chemotaxis/respiratory burst and granule release. IL-10 from T cells inhibits activated macrophages/dendritic cells, IL-12 production, costimulators and class II MHC expression.

pages.title: Arachidonic acid pathways and inhibitors
pages.visualNotes: Pathway: membrane phospholipids -> phospholipase A2 -> arachidonic acid; glucocorticoids inhibit upstream. 5-lipoxygenase (inhibited by zileuton) -> leukotrienes; montelukast/zafirlukast antagonize leukotriene receptors. LTC4/LTD4/LTE4 increase bronchial tone; LTB4 increases neutrophil chemotaxis. Cyclooxygenase: celecoxib COX2; aspirin irreversible and other NSAIDs reversible inhibit COX1/2. PGI2 decreases platelet aggregation and vascular tone; PGE1 decreases vascular tone; PGE2/PGF2alpha increase uterine tone; TXA2 increases platelet aggregation and vascular tone. Named analogues: epoprostenol, alprostadil, dinoprostone, carboprost.

pages.title: Arachidonic acid pathway illustration
pages.visualNotes: Diagram: phospholipase A2 (corticosteroids inhibit; calcium enhances) releases arachidonic acid from phospholipids; linoleic acid -> arachidonic acid. 5-lipoxygenase -> LTB4/LTC4/LTD4/LTE4 (group labeled bronchoconstrictors), and LXA4/LXB4. Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase; montelukast inhibits LTC/D/E4 receptors. Cyclooxygenase -> PGG2 -> PGH2 -> TXA2 via platelet thromboxane synthase (aggregation, vasoconstriction); PGI2 via endothelial prostacyclin synthase (inhibits aggregation, vasodilator; dipyridamole enhances). PGD2/PGE2/PGF2 also shown. Aspirin label: irreversible, 3–5 days to reverse platelet effect (must synthesize enzyme); NSAIDs reversible, <24 hours.

pages.title: Plasma mediator cascades
pages.visualNotes: Four plasma cascades linked by factor XII/Hageman activation on collagen, basement membrane, activated platelets, with HMWK cofactor. XIIa converts prekallikrein to kallikrein, which feeds back to XII and cleaves HMWK to bradykinin. Clotting cascade XIIa -> XIa -> Xa -> thrombin from prothrombin; thrombin forms fibrin from fibrinogen and fibrinopeptides, activates protease-activated receptors to inflammation. Kallikrein forms plasmin from plasminogen; plasmin causes fibrin split products and complement cleavage C3 -> C3a. Bradykinin: permeability, vasodilation, pain; thrombin: adhesion, permeability, chemotaxis; C3a: permeability.

pages.title: Outcome table
pages.visualNotes: Outcome table: persistent acute inflammation remains active without resolution or chronic progression (IL8). Resolution with regeneration: macrophages remove debris/pathogen, lymphatics resorb edema, stem cells proliferate (IL10,TGFbeta). Resolution with scarring: debris/pathogen/edema cleared but insufficient stem cells; fibrotic replacement (PDGF,FGF2,TGFbeta). Abscess: pus/tissue necrosis, fibrous separation from healthy tissue; septic infectious or sterile noninfectious after persistent injected substances (glucocorticoids,synthol,oils) or formerly septic abscess after pathogen cleared (IL1beta,TNFalpha). Chronic: persistent cause, macrophage/APC presentation to helper T cells, CD4+ infiltration (IL1,TNFalpha,IL12,IL6).

pages.title: Outcome pathways
pages.visualNotes: Flowchart: injury (infarction,bacteria,toxins,trauma) -> acute inflammation (vascular changes,neutrophils,mediators); resolution clears stimuli/mediators/cells,replaces injured cells, restores function. Abscess heals by scar; acute can heal by scar or progress chronic. Chronic stimuli include viruses,chronic infections,persistent injury,autoimmune disease. Chronic has angiogenesis, mononuclear cells,fibrosis; can heal by scar (dense fibrosis,loss of function) or regeneration (clearance,remodeling,normal function).

pages.title: Expanded granulomatous etiologies
pages.visualNotes: Table infectious etiologies: mycobacteria (tuberculosis,leprosy),Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch,stellate necrotizing granulomas),Listeria monocytogenes (granulomatosis infantiseptica),Treponema pallidum (tertiary syphilis); endemic mycoses e.g.histoplasmosis; schistosomiasis; catalase-positive organisms in chronic granulomatous disease. Noninfectious: immune-mediated sarcoidosis,Crohn disease,primary biliary cholangitis,subacute de Quervain/granulomatous thyroiditis; vasculitis—granulomatosis with polyangiitis,eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis,giant-cell temporal arteritis,Takayasu arteritis; foreign bodies—berylliosis,talcosis,hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

pages.title: Caseous and noncaseating granulomas
pages.visualNotes: Early granuloma labels lymphocytes and macrophages. Caseous epithelioid granuloma labels fibroblasts producing collagen,lymphocytes/plasma cells,Langhans giant cell,epithelioid macrophages and caseous necrosis. Noncaseating epithelioid granuloma shown separately. Figure equates caseous with infectious and noncaseating with noninfectious; this is retained as a source overgeneralization and not scored as universal.

uncertainties.description: Diagram equates infectious granulomas with caseation and noninfectious with noncaseation; etiologic tables p36/37 are broader. Do not score as universal diagnostic rule.
